h: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר, מַאֲמָר ט׳ Rosh Chodesh Adar — Maamar Tes

p: "Just as when Av enters we diminish joy,
so when Adar enters we increase joy."
That is: just as in Av,
because of one day that befell in it,
we diminish joy from Rosh Chodesh,
so in Adar, because of the days of Purim,
we increase joy from Rosh Chodesh.
"A person is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim
And we do not find at any time
that there is a mitzvah in drunkenness
And the reason is to show
that Yisrael are bound, beyond awareness,
at the root, in the very beginning of the Thought;
and this stands against the kelipah of Amalek,
who is the "first" of the kelipah,
and he opposes the holiness of the bris
for an infant is circumcised without awareness
and enters the category of "And your people, etc.,
so that he has a share in Olam HaBa;
that they are not all righteous.
And the mitzvah comes against this
with drunkenness and joy beyond awareness;
"They reel and stagger like a drunkard";
and this is the revelation of joy,
which is forbidden in this world.
that the revelation of joy will be only in the future,
when there will be a revelation of Atika.
And at the time of Amalek's eradication
there is a revelation of Atika,
and the revelation of joy was permitted,
and on the contrary, there is a mitzvah in it.
And this is why we increase from Rosh Chodesh,
regarding what he said in Sefer Yetzirah,
that the work of this month is
that even laughter is in holiness,
And this is what they said, "we increase joy,"
at the beginning of the chapter Ein Omdin
where he said, "I am wearing tefillin,"
And the version of the Ein Yaakov is:
But in truth we do not find
any difference in the laws of mourning
for one obligated in it, Heaven spare us,
in Adar as against the rest of the year.
Rather, its meaning appears to be
that we diminish the well-known mourning,
which is the mourning for Tziyon and Yerushalayim.
And this is according to what they said
merits to see its joy, etc."
and did not merit to see its joy!
And if it refers to Techiyas HaMeisim,
that they will rise and see its joy —
except those listed in Perek Chelek
and Techiyas HaMeisim and Olam HaBa
And we said that the intent is
that he merits to see its joy
in the present, in our time,
along the lines of what they said (Berachos 33a):
it is as if the Beis HaMikdash was built in his days."
except at the time when Yisrael
are in the Holy Land, etc.;
here, at the time when Yisrael
dwell in the Holy Land, etc.
And in this month He made Kuf king,
which alludes to the upper and lower holiness,
the Written Torah and Torah she'b'al peh.
they accepted it anew in the days of Achashverosh
לֹא הָיָה עַל יְדֵי כְּפִיַּת הַר כְּגִיגִית
was not through the mountain held over them like a barrel,
for at Matan Torah they said,
"We will do and we will hear,"
And it is written, "Through wisdom a house is built, etc.,
and through knowledge the chambers are filled
as they expounded in the Midrash
this is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues.
which comes from joining the wisdom in the mind
to the understanding in the heart,
along the lines of what it says
and knowledge is pleasant to your soul"
And it is the time to merit
that it be as if there were built
the Beis HaMikdash in one's days,
and we merit to see its joy
in the present, even in exile;
and we diminish the mourning for Tziyon and Yerushalayim
And this is what they said,
And on Shabbos all Yisrael merit
the spreading of the shelter of peace
and the holiness of Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash.
And talmidei chachamim, who are likened to Shabbosos
and it is as if the Beis HaMikdash was built in their days.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 7b — “Rava said: A person is obligated to become mellow with wine on Purim until he does not know the difference between Cursed is Haman and Blessed is Mordechai.” Rav Tzadok is interpreting the state beyond ordinary awareness as a spiritual level. The following narrative in the Gemara records the danger at Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira's feast; the passage is not an unrestricted endorsement of intoxication.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rav Tzadok HaKohen, Resisei Layla 20 — “This holiness is revealed with all its force on Purim, when they said that one must become mellow until he does not know. Its plain meaning is the revelation that Israel's hearts are truly attached to the blessed God even when they cannot distinguish their right from their left. ... Then what lies in the depths of the heart is revealed. Israel's hearts are attached to the blessed God without deliberation or compulsion of the heart's will: the point of true will is of itself truly attached to Him.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Resisei Layla explains what the loss of ordinary calculation discloses: an enduring inner will attached to God. It clarifies why Rav Tzadok relates Purim's joy to the root of Israel's holiness rather than to a new intellectual achievement.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Purim 5634 (1874), s.v. Teshuasam Hayisa LaNetzach — “'You were their salvation forever, and their hope in every generation.' The salvation of Purim was for all generations. Just as the decree was to destroy all the Jews, so the miracle concerned every generation: the continued existence of all Israel's descendants rests on this miracle. It is taught that the decree also existed in Heaven against Israel. The Holy One, blessed be He, performed the miracle without Israel's merit, solely because we are His people and always take refuge in Him; therefore He must save us in a time of distress. This festival thus gives Israel strength and hope in exile to trust Him because we belong uniquely to Him. It seems that for this reason they instituted becoming intoxicated 'until one does not know': to show that the festival does not rest on Israel's merit. It is called Purim after the lot because the lot signifies what the natural circumstances and the power the other side acquired through our sins would have brought about; only through His kindness did Hashem save us.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Sefat Emet connects this particular Purim practice to the ground of the salvation: Israel's enduring belonging to Hashem reaches beyond the account of its conduct that supported the decree. This gives a precise counterpart to Rav Tzadok's argument that Amalek challenges a holiness conferred before conscious choice, and that the mitzvah performed beyond ordinary awareness answers that challenge. Sefat Emet does not discuss circumcision here; his contribution is the distinction between belonging and the merit being judged.

paragraphs.text: Ein Yaakov, Taanis 29a — “Rav Yehudah, son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, said in Rav's name: Just as, when Av enters, we reduce joy, so, when Adar enters, we reduce mourning and increase joy.” The Vilna text of Taanis 29a reads only “so, when Adar enters, we increase joy” (מַרְבִּין בְּשִׂמְחָה). The Ein Yaakov adds the words “we reduce mourning” (מְמַעֲטִין בְּאֵבֶל) before “and increase joy,” and spells the verb מרבים. The Glick edition of Ein Yaakov follows the Bavli and lacks the addition. Rav Tzadok quotes the Ein Yaakov reading and then explains which mourning is meant.

paragraphs.text: Taanit 30b — “The Sages say: Whoever works on Tishah B'Av and does not mourn for Jerusalem does not see her joy, as it is said, Rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all who love her; rejoice with her in gladness, all who mourn over her. From here they said: Whoever mourns for Jerusalem merits and sees her joy; whoever does not mourn for Jerusalem does not see her joy.” The wording is merits and sees, in the present tense. Rav Tzadok reads this as an inward participation in Jerusalem's joy even before the final rebuilding.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Devarim 16 — “The intent is that he merits and sees: even at the time of mourning he feels the illumination of the joy, like the Arab who, at the Destruction, sensed that Mashiach had been born.” Rav Tzadok gives a concrete model for joy “in the present.” It is a joy felt within the mourning itself, the redemption perceived at the very hour of loss (Eichah Rabbah 1).

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 43 — “Through joining Chochmah, the mind, and Binah, the heart … it is as if the Beis HaMikdash was built in his days — that is, his heart becomes a Beis HaMikdash.” This explains why daas brings “as if the Mikdash were built.” The bond of mind and heart turns the heart itself into the dwelling place of the Shechinah, so its joy can be felt even in exile.

paragraphs.text: ZoharIII 124b, Nasso 6:93 — “When the tree of good and evil rules—ordinary things of purity and ordinary things of impurity—the sages, who resemble Shabbosos and festivals, have only what those ordinary people give them, just as Shabbos has only what is prepared for it during the weekdays.” The Zohar compares Torah sages with Shabbos in its discussion of their sustenance. Rav Tzadok develops the comparison as continual participation in Shabbos holiness.
